title: Beyond RAG: Build a Relational Context Engine from Scratch — Peter Werry, Unblocked
talk_summary: Peter Werry shows how to build a 'relational context engine' that complements vector RAG by having an LLM translate natural language into validated, schema-aware database queries (e.g., MongoDB) over structured engineering data like PRs. The reusable core is a pipeline of schema discovery, identity resolution, allow-list validation, and an error-feedback retry loop, all wrapped in procedural code rather than trusting the LLM.

takeaways.technique: LLM writes structured queries instead of stuffing retrieved docs
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of embedding a query and stuffing top-K docs into the prompt, the model emits a real DB query (filters, state, temporal, sort/limit) against a known schema, so structural/temporal questions ('PRs I merged last week') are answered exactly rather than by semantic near-miss.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the model doesn't actually answer the question in this paradigm. It writes the query that accesses the database.

takeaways.what_they_do: They pass the (markdown) schema and the current date/time into the prompt so the model can generate correct temporal and field-scoped queries.
takeaways.evidence_quote: LLMs are actually pretty good about generating temporal queries if you pass them the current date and time.

takeaways.what_they_do: Model output is validated against an allow-list of operators/fields (deny by default), blocking dangerous operators (e.g. $where executing JS) and hidden metadata fields; validation is procedural code, not an LLM.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we don't deny list these things. We allow list them. So, it's deny by default.

takeaways.what_they_do: If the generated query fails validation or execution, the error is fed back to the LLM to self-correct, bounded by a max-attempts cap.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we can take that error and pass it back into the LLM and say hey that was wrong... up to some number of max attempts

takeaways.what_they_do: Map human names to canonical IDs (e.g. 'Peter' -> GitHub login) via fuzzy matching (Levenshtein) before querying, so name-based queries don't silently return nothing.
takeaways.evidence_quote: without doing some sort of identity mapping it would just say... it would just match across Peter and it's not going to find anything.

takeaways.technique: Schema summarization to shave context at scale
takeaways.what_they_do: For many tables/collections, attach tiny summaries/descriptions to each schema and use an LLM step to load only the relevant schema for the query, instead of dumping all schemas into the prompt.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the schema collections have tiny little summaries and descriptions and then... depending on what the query is, you can load the right schema for that query.
